chapter: Quality Serenaders, Cotton Club and union recollections
title: His own tone and how audiences received his solos
summary: Howard says people called his tone beautiful, but he felt his solo playing often did not get across.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: What about your sound at that time, were you a strong player, too?
What about the other people that were listening? Did they always say you had a big tone?
They always said I had a beautiful tone.

You said something about that one period, just a few minutes ago, that somebody didn't like your playing, the people. What did you mean by that? Were you playing something that was a little different than what they had been used to hearing? You know what I'm saying? Did you have a style all of your own that they didn't quite understand or something?
When you said they didn't like you, it seems like to me from what we've heard and what we've read, everybody seemed to like Paul Howard and the Quality Serenaders.
Oh, yeah, they liked it all right.
Well, did you feel that your own solo playing wasn't getting across to them?
You were just like a very sensitive player.
When you'd play would you look for a little reaction from the people, or --
Oh, yeah, there was a reaction from the people, and like by that way I could --
You could tell how you were doing.
Tell how I was doing, yeah.
I see. Well, apparently you sounded great, because everybody that heard you was impressed.
What about the records that you made, were you happy with what you sounded like when they --
Did that make you feel a little more confident about your playing?
Yeah, much more. When I got so I --
You were always sort of a modest gentleman at that period, and now too.
Okay. You mean you've changed your attitude.
Trying and trying and trying. Try anybody. Try anything.
